cards.statement: React interprets a capitalized JSX tag as a reference to a component function.
cards.explanation: A tag such as <Profile /> refers to the Profile component; lowercase tags represent built-in elements.

cards.statement: Defining a component inside another component preserves its identity across parent renders.
cards.explanation: A nested definition creates a new component function when the parent renders. React treats it as a different component, which can reset its state.
cards.misconception: A nested component definition retains its identity between parent renders.

cards.statement: A named component export is imported with a bare identifier after import.
cards.explanation: A named component export uses a named import such as import { Profile } from './Profile.js'. A bare identifier imports a default export.
cards.misconception: Named and default component exports use the same import syntax.

cards.statement: Two adjacent JSX tags returned by a component need one wrapping parent tag or a Fragment.
cards.explanation: JSX turns into plain JavaScript objects, and a function returns one value, so adjacent tags go inside one parent such as a <div> or <>...</>.

cards.statement: A Fragment groups sibling JSX elements and renders their DOM nodes directly.
cards.explanation: A Fragment provides a JSX parent while adding no wrapper element to the browser's DOM tree.

cards.statement: JSX accepts an unclosed tag when the browser treats it as a void element.
cards.explanation: JSX requires explicit closing syntax, including for a self-closing tag.
cards.misconception: HTML's void-element syntax works unchanged in JSX.

cards.statement: In JSX, the SVG stroke-width attribute is written as strokeWidth.
cards.explanation: Many HTML and SVG attributes use camelCase in JSX because their names become JavaScript object keys.

cards.statement: In React's JSX convention, a DOM element's CSS class is written with the HTML attribute name class.
cards.explanation: Because class is a reserved word in JavaScript, React writes className in JSX, named after the corresponding DOM property.
cards.misconception: The HTML class attribute keeps the same name in JSX.

cards.statement: JSX expects a CSS declaration string in a DOM element's style prop.
cards.explanation: The JSX style prop takes a JavaScript object, such as style={{ backgroundColor: 'black' }}.
cards.misconception: Inline styles in JSX use the same declaration string as HTML.

source.title: JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces

cards.statement: Returning null from a function component renders nothing in that component's place.
cards.explanation: A component has to return something, so when a condition means it should show nothing, it returns null instead of JSX.

cards.statement: In JSX, count && <Badge /> hides the expression when count is 0.
cards.explanation: When count is 0, the && expression evaluates to 0, and React renders that 0. Use a boolean condition such as count > 0.
cards.misconception: A falsy number on the left of && disappears from JSX.

cards.statement: A function component receives each JSX prop as a separate positional argument.
cards.explanation: React supplies a single props object to a function component. The component can read its properties or destructure them.
cards.misconception: React calls a component with one function argument per prop.

cards.statement: A destructured prop default replaces null with the fallback value.
cards.explanation: A default parameter value applies when the prop is missing or undefined. An explicit null remains null.
cards.misconception: Destructuring defaults treat null like an omitted prop.

cards.statement: Nested JSX inside a custom component becomes that component's children prop.
cards.explanation: For <Card><Avatar /></Card>, Card receives <Avatar /> as its children prop and can choose where to render it.

cards.statement: A child component can edit the props object it receives to update its parent.
cards.explanation: Props are read-only snapshots. To change what a child receives, its parent supplies new prop values on a later render.
cards.misconception: Mutating received props communicates a change back to the parent.

cards.statement: A parent can pass a callback function as a prop for a child to call during an interaction.
cards.explanation: Custom component props can hold JavaScript functions, letting a child call behavior supplied by its parent.

cards.statement: Writing <Avatar {...props} /> forwards every prop a component received to Avatar.
cards.explanation: JSX spread syntax passes a component's props on without listing each name. React's docs advise using it with restraint.

cards.statement: Custom component props are limited to the attributes supported by DOM elements.
cards.explanation: Your own components can accept prop names you define. Built-in DOM elements have predefined supported props.
cards.misconception: Custom components share the DOM element attribute list.

cards.statement: In React 19, function components receive ref as a regular prop.
cards.explanation: React 19 lets a function component read ref from its props, so forwardRef is no longer needed for that purpose.

cards.statement: In React 19, defaultProps still supplies defaults for function components.
cards.explanation: React 19 removed defaultProps support for function components; use default parameter values instead. Class components still support defaultProps.
cards.misconception: Function components retain defaultProps support in React 19.

cards.statement: In React 19, React runs propTypes checks for function components in development.
cards.explanation: React 19 ignores propTypes checks rather than running them in development.
cards.misconception: React 19 still performs runtime propTypes checks for function components.

cards.statement: On a re-render, React starts by calling the component whose state update triggered it.
cards.explanation: React calls the root component for the initial render. A later render begins with the function component whose state update set it off.

cards.statement: During rendering, React calls component functions to determine their JSX output.
cards.explanation: Rendering is the calculation phase in which React calls components to find out what they return.

cards.statement: React skips child component functions by default when their parent re-renders.
cards.explanation: By default, React renders components nested inside the updated component. Optimizations can skip some of that work.
cards.misconception: Unchanged child props automatically prevent child rendering.

cards.statement: On the initial commit, React appends newly created DOM nodes to the target container.
cards.explanation: React creates DOM nodes for the initial render and places them in the DOM during commit.

cards.statement: React changes the DOM after a re-render even when the rendered output stays the same.
cards.explanation: React leaves DOM nodes alone when a re-render produces the same output as the previous render.
cards.misconception: Every React re-render forces a matching DOM update.

cards.statement: React's render tree includes host elements such as div and img alongside components.
cards.explanation: The render tree is composed only of React components. Host elements such as div or img are platform UI primitives, so the render tree leaves them out.
cards.misconception: Every HTML element a component returns becomes a node in the render tree.

source.title: Understanding Your UI as a Tree

cards.statement: In the render tree, a component passed as children sits under the component that receives those children.
cards.explanation: If App imports Copyright but passes it as children to InspirationGenerator, the render tree puts Copyright under InspirationGenerator, while the module dependency tree puts it under App.

source.title: Understanding Your UI as a Tree

cards.statement: Pushing items into an array created during the same render keeps a component pure.
cards.explanation: Mutating an array created within the current render is local mutation; the array starts fresh on the next render.

cards.statement: The Rules of React allow a component to send an analytics event while it renders.
cards.explanation: Sending an analytics event is a side effect. React can render a component more than once, so side effects belong in event handlers or, as a last resort, an Effect.
cards.misconception: Sending analytics while rendering is fine under the Rules of React.

source.title: Components and Hooks must be pure

cards.statement: useState returns the current state value and a setter function for requesting its next value.
cards.explanation: The two-item array from useState contains the value for the current render and its corresponding set function.

cards.statement: A local variable in a function component persists between renders like useState data.
cards.explanation: React runs the component function again on a re-render, recreating its local variables. useState retains data between renders.
cards.misconception: Ordinary local variables provide the same component memory as state.

cards.statement: An event handler reads a new state value immediately after calling its state setter.
cards.explanation: A state setter affects the next render. The event handler still reads the state snapshot from the render that created it.
cards.misconception: Calling a state setter mutates the state variable in the running handler.

cards.statement: React batches state updates queued during the same event handler.
cards.explanation: React processes queued updates after the event handler finishes, avoiding a render between its individual setter calls.

source.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates

cards.statement: An updater function receives the pending state produced by earlier updates in the same queue.
cards.explanation: React passes each queued updater the pending value left by the preceding update, then uses its return value for the next one.

source.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates

cards.statement: React skips re-rendering a component's children when the new state is Object.is-equal to the current one.
cards.explanation: The set function compares the new and current state with Object.is. React may still call the component itself before skipping its children.

cards.statement: Setting an object state variable with a partial object merges its fields into the prior object.
cards.explanation: A useState setter replaces the object value. Copy the previous fields explicitly, for example with object spread.
cards.misconception: useState merges partial object updates automatically.

cards.statement: Updating a nested object in state involves copying the path to the changed property.
cards.explanation: Object spread is shallow, so an immutable nested update copies the outer object and each nested object along the changed path.

cards.statement: Calling sort() on an array held in state leaves the previous state array intact.
cards.explanation: sort() mutates its array. Copy an array held in state before sorting the copy.
cards.misconception: Array sort() returns a sorted result while preserving the input array.

cards.statement: Passing createItems() to useState defers that call until state initialization.
cards.explanation: JavaScript calls createItems() while evaluating the argument on each render. Passing createItems as an initializer lets React call it during initialization.
cards.misconception: React lazily evaluates a function call passed as the initial state value.

cards.statement: The setter returned by useState keeps the same identity across renders.
cards.explanation: React provides a stable set function for a state variable, so its identity does not change when the component re-renders.

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends grouping state values that change together.
cards.explanation: When values change together, grouping them in one state variable helps keep their updates in sync.

cards.statement: In a normalized state shape, a parent item holds its children's full objects in an array.
cards.explanation: Flat, or normalized, state gives a parent an array of child IDs and keeps a separate mapping from each ID to its item, which makes nested updates easier.
cards.misconception: Flattening state means a parent still holds its children's full objects.

cards.statement: Sibling components share state when their closest common parent owns it.
cards.explanation: Lifting state to a common parent lets that parent pass the current value and update handlers to the siblings.

cards.statement: A controlled component receives its important value through props from its parent.
cards.explanation: A component is described as controlled when its important information is driven by parent-supplied props.

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends one reducer action per user interaction, even when it changes several fields.
cards.explanation: Resetting a five-field form dispatches one reset_form action rather than five set_field actions, so a log of actions shows what the user actually did.

source.title: Extracting State Logic into a Reducer

cards.statement: Switching between {isA && <Counter />} and {!isA && <Counter />} carries Counter's state across.
cards.explanation: Each && expression is its own slot in the render tree, so the two Counters sit at different positions and React destroys the state of the one that is removed.
cards.misconception: State belongs to a JSX tag independently of its tree position.

cards.statement: Replacing a component type at the same tree position preserves the previous type's state.
cards.explanation: When a different component type occupies the same position, React removes the old component and discards its state.
cards.misconception: Tree position alone preserves state when the component type changes.

cards.statement: useReducer returns the current state and a dispatch function.
cards.explanation: A component reads the state returned by useReducer and passes an action to dispatch to request its next state.

cards.statement: A reducer may read a changing global counter when computing state from an action.
cards.explanation: Reducers must be pure: the same state and action should produce the same next state. A changing global counter makes the result depend on another input.
cards.misconception: A reducer may depend on mutable global data while remaining pure.

source.title: Extracting State Logic into a Reducer

cards.statement: A component renders an array of JSX elements returned by map().
cards.explanation: Mapping data items to JSX creates an array that a component can include in its returned UI.

cards.statement: A key on a nested <li> satisfies the key needed by its mapped <Row /> parent.
cards.explanation: The element returned directly from map() needs the key. For a mapped <Row />, place key on <Row />, rather than on an <li> inside Row.
cards.misconception: A key anywhere inside a mapped component identifies that mapped component.

cards.statement: React requires list keys to be unique across unrelated arrays in the same app.
cards.explanation: Keys identify items among siblings. Separate arrays can reuse the same key values.
cards.misconception: A key must be globally unique across a React application.

cards.statement: A UUID generated when a local item is created provides a stable key for that item.
cards.explanation: For locally created data, generate an ID when the item is created and keep it with that item across renders.

cards.statement: Using array indexes as keys preserves item identity when a list is reordered.
cards.explanation: An index describes a position, which changes when items move. Index keys can associate existing UI state with the wrong item.
cards.misconception: An item's array index stays a reliable identity through reordering.

cards.statement: Random keys generated during rendering make React recreate list items on each render.
cards.explanation: When keys change on each render, React cannot match list items to their previous instances and recreates their components and DOM.

cards.statement: The short <>...</> Fragment syntax accepts a key for items returned by map().
cards.explanation: The short Fragment syntax has no place for a key. Use the explicit <Fragment key={id}> syntax for a keyed multi-element item.
cards.misconception: Short Fragment syntax accepts attributes such as key.

cards.statement: A component receives its key value through props.key during rendering.
cards.explanation: React uses key as its own hint and does not pass it to the component. Pass an ID separately if the component needs it.
cards.misconception: key is an ordinary component prop.

cards.statement: Changing a component's key tells React to recreate it with fresh state.
cards.explanation: A different key makes React treat the component as a new instance, resetting the state in that subtree.

cards.statement: When a mapped element omits key, React identifies it by its data object's ID.
cards.explanation: When key is omitted, React uses the item's array index as its key; it does not inspect the data object's ID.
cards.misconception: React automatically finds an ID property when key is omitted.

cards.statement: The default value passed to createContext tracks the latest provider value.
cards.explanation: A context's default value is a static fallback used when a reader has no matching provider above it.
cards.misconception: createContext stores a changing global copy of the provider's value.

cards.statement: When providers are nested, useContext selects the outermost matching value.
cards.explanation: useContext reads the value from the closest matching provider above the component.
cards.misconception: The first provider near the root takes priority over nested providers.

cards.statement: A provider returned by a component changes that component's own useContext read.
cards.explanation: A component's useContext call reads providers above that component. A provider in its returned JSX applies to descendants.
cards.misconception: A provider affects a useContext call in the component that returns it.

cards.statement: In React 19, <ThemeContext value={theme}> supplies context to its descendants.
cards.explanation: React 19 lets a context object render directly as its provider. <ThemeContext.Provider> remains the legacy provider form.

cards.statement: Changing a provider's value causes React to re-render descendants that read that context.
cards.explanation: React updates components reading a context when their provider supplies a different value.

cards.statement: React compares a provider's previous and next context values with Object.is.
cards.explanation: React uses Object.is to determine whether the provider's context value changed between renders.

cards.statement: Wrapping a context reader in memo blocks updates from its provider.
cards.explanation: memo cannot block a component from receiving a changed context value from its provider.
cards.misconception: memo prevents context-driven re-renders as well as prop-driven ones.

cards.statement: In React 19, the use API reads context inside a conditional branch.
cards.explanation: Unlike a Hook, the use API may be called in a condition or loop to read a context when that branch runs.

cards.statement: In React 19, a Server Component can read context through the use API during rendering.
cards.explanation: Reading context with use is unsupported in Server Components. This limitation concerns the context form of use.
cards.misconception: The use API reads context in Server Components as it does in Client Components.

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends using context first when props cross several component levels.
cards.explanation: React's documentation recommends starting with props. Passing data through several levels alone does not require context.
cards.misconception: Prop drilling automatically makes context the recommended first choice.

cards.statement: useRef returns a mutable object whose initial value appears in current.
cards.explanation: The object returned by useRef has a current property initialized from the value passed to useRef.

cards.statement: Changing ref.current requests a component re-render like a state setter.
cards.explanation: Changing ref.current does not trigger a re-render; React does not track writes to the plain ref object.
cards.misconception: Ref writes notify React of a UI update.

cards.statement: A useRef object keeps the same identity across its component's renders.
cards.explanation: React returns the same ref object on later renders, so current retains information between them.

cards.statement: Reading ref.current during render is a supported way to calculate JSX.
cards.explanation: React advises against reading or writing ref.current while calculating JSX. Use state for values that drive rendering.
cards.misconception: A mutable ref is a normal render input.

cards.statement: React sets a DOM ref's current value after committing its node.
cards.explanation: React assigns the corresponding DOM node to ref.current during the commit, after updating the DOM.

cards.statement: A DOM ref retains its node in current after React removes that node.
cards.explanation: React sets an object ref's current property back to null when its DOM node is removed.
cards.misconception: Object refs keep detached DOM nodes until application code clears them.

cards.statement: In React 19, a ref callback can return a cleanup function for detach.
cards.explanation: React 19 calls a ref callback's returned cleanup function when it detaches that ref.

cards.statement: In React 19, a ref callback that returns no cleanup skips any detach notification.
cards.explanation: If a ref callback returns no cleanup function, React 19 calls that callback with null when detaching the ref.
cards.misconception: Ref callbacks need an explicit cleanup return to receive detach notification.
cards.volatilityNote: The React documentation says the null-on-detach fallback will be removed in a future version.

cards.statement: useImperativeHandle sets the parent's ref to the value that createHandle returns.
cards.explanation: The parent gets your custom handle, so a component can expose only chosen methods, such as focus and scrollIntoView, and keep its DOM node private.

cards.statement: flushSync from react-dom commits updates in its callback before the next line runs.
cards.explanation: flushSync forces updates inside its callback to flush synchronously, leaving the DOM updated when execution continues.

cards.statement: React runs an Effect's setup while calculating the component's JSX.
cards.explanation: React runs Effect setup after the component commits. Calculating JSX happens during rendering.
cards.misconception: Effect setup is part of rendering.

cards.statement: React runs an Effect's previous cleanup before setup with changed dependencies.
cards.explanation: When dependencies change, React cleans up synchronization using the old values before setting it up with the new values.

cards.statement: React runs a provided Effect cleanup when the component unmounts.
cards.explanation: A cleanup function returned from Effect setup stops or undoes its synchronization when the component leaves the page.

cards.statement: An Effect can omit a prop read by its setup from the dependency array when that prop changes rarely.
cards.explanation: An Effect's dependency array includes reactive values its setup reads, including props. How often a prop changes does not remove that dependency.
cards.misconception: Rarely changing props may be omitted from Effect dependencies.

cards.statement: An Effect with [] dependencies re-runs whenever its component updates state.
cards.explanation: An empty dependency array keeps state and prop updates from re-synchronizing that Effect.
cards.misconception: An empty dependency array behaves like an omitted dependency array.

cards.statement: React generally runs Effects after paint for updates outside user interactions.
cards.explanation: For an update unrelated to an interaction, React generally lets the browser paint the updated screen before running the Effect.

cards.statement: Server rendering runs useEffect setup after generating HTML.
cards.explanation: Effects run on the client. Server rendering does not execute useEffect setup.
cards.misconception: Server rendering runs Effects after producing HTML.

cards.statement: useLayoutEffect runs before the browser paints the updated screen.
cards.explanation: useLayoutEffect runs after the DOM commit and before repaint, making it suitable for layout measurements that affect the visible result.

cards.statement: Since React 19.2, useEffectEvent reads current props without resynchronizing its Effect.
cards.explanation: An Effect Event sees the latest committed props and state while its surrounding Effect remains reactive only to its own dependencies.

cards.statement: An Effect that copies a derived value into state can save a render pass.
cards.explanation: Copying a calculated value into state from an Effect adds a render with the stale value, then another with the updated value. Calculate it during rendering.
cards.misconception: An Effect makes derived display state cheaper to update.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends separate Effects for unrelated synchronization processes.
cards.explanation: Separate Effects let each synchronization process react to its own dependencies. A change to one process need not restart another.

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends notifying a parent of a toggle through an Effect.
cards.explanation: For a toggle caused by an interaction, call the parent's callback during the same event that updates the child.
cards.misconception: An Effect is the preferred place to report an interaction to a parent.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: For an external store, React's documentation recommends a purpose-built Hook over an Effect that copies it into state.
cards.explanation: React provides useSyncExternalStore as a purpose-built Hook for subscribing to data outside React, preferred over an Effect that copies the store into state.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: getSnapshot may return a fresh object on repeated calls while its store stays unchanged.
cards.explanation: While the store is unchanged, getSnapshot must return the same value. A mutable store needs a cached immutable snapshot.
cards.misconception: A newly allocated but equivalent snapshot is safe on each read.

cards.statement: An Effect fetching data can use cleanup to prevent a stale response from updating state.
cards.explanation: The cleanup can mark an earlier request as obsolete; its response handler then ignores the result instead of overwriting newer data.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: An Effect that updates messages with setMessages(msgs => [...msgs, msg]) depends on messages.
cards.explanation: With an updater function, the Effect never reads the messages variable, so messages leaves its dependency list and a new message no longer re-runs the Effect.
cards.misconception: Updating a state variable from an Effect makes it a dependency even through an updater.

cards.statement: Declaring a helper function inside an Effect removes it from the Effect's dependency list.
cards.explanation: A function declared inside the Effect is part of its setup rather than a reactive value created during component rendering.

cards.statement: Two components calling the same custom Hook can share the Hook's local useState state.
cards.explanation: Each call to a custom Hook has independent local state. Reusing the Hook's code does not merge its callers' useState values.
cards.misconception: Calling the same custom Hook shares one local state cell.

cards.statement: useMemo keeps a cached value when an object dependency has equal contents but a new identity.
cards.explanation: useMemo compares dependencies with Object.is. A newly created object differs from the prior object even when their fields match.
cards.misconception: useMemo compares object dependencies by their contents.

cards.statement: useCallback usually returns the previous function while dependencies remain equal.
cards.explanation: useCallback caches a function value between renders until its dependencies change.

cards.statement: memo compares the whole props object by reference before skipping a render.
cards.explanation: By default, memo compares each prop with Object.is. The props object itself is not the unit of comparison.
cards.misconception: memo requires the entire props object to retain one identity.

cards.statement: memo guarantees a stable-props child skips its render function.
cards.explanation: memo usually skips a parent-driven re-render when props stay equal, but React may still render the component. It is a performance optimization.
cards.misconception: memo provides a semantic guarantee that rendering is skipped.

cards.statement: memo accepts an arePropsEqual function to compare a component's old and new props.
cards.explanation: An optional arePropsEqual function tells memo whether the previous and next props produce the same output and behavior.

cards.statement: React Compiler analyzes and rewrites components while they render in the browser.
cards.explanation: React Compiler is a build-time tool: it analyzes and transforms components during the build, and the browser runs the compiled output.
cards.misconception: React Compiler performs its analysis during browser rendering.

cards.statement: React Compiler can memoize calculations inside compiled custom Hooks.
cards.explanation: React Compiler applies memoization within React Hooks as well as components, including calculations they perform during rendering.

cards.statement: React Compiler shares one memoized calculation across separate components.
cards.explanation: React Compiler's memoization is local to a component or Hook. It does not share one cached result across separate components.
cards.misconception: Compiler-generated caches are shared across component boundaries.

cards.statement: React Compiler accepts useMemo and useCallback as escape hatches for precise memoization.
cards.explanation: With React Compiler enabled, useMemo and useCallback still provide explicit control over which values are memoized.

cards.statement: useCallback invokes the supplied function during the render that declares it.
cards.explanation: useCallback returns the function value; it does not call that function. The caller decides when to invoke it.
cards.misconception: useCallback executes its argument while rendering.

cards.statement: Typing into an input interrupts a chart re-render that React is running as a Transition.
cards.explanation: Transition updates are interruptible: React handles the urgent input update first, then restarts the chart's rendering work.

cards.statement: In React 19, useTransition's isPending first turns true when the async Action resolves.
cards.explanation: isPending flips to true as soon as startTransition is first called, and goes back to false once the Action finishes and its final state is on screen.
cards.misconception: An async Action becomes pending only after its Promise resolves.

cards.statement: In React 19, useActionState returns state, an Action dispatcher, and a pending flag.
cards.explanation: useActionState returns the current state, a dispatchAction function, and an isPending value for its dispatched Actions.

cards.statement: In React 19, a useActionState Action receives FormData as its first argument.
cards.explanation: The Action passed to useActionState receives previous state first. When used for a form, submitted FormData follows it.
cards.misconception: A useActionState form Action receives FormData before previous state.

cards.statement: In React 19, a function passed to a form's action prop receives submitted FormData.
cards.explanation: A function used as a form action handles the submission in a Transition and receives the submitted form data.

cards.statement: In React 19, a submit button's formAction function runs alongside the form's action function.
cards.explanation: A submit button's formAction overrides the enclosing form's action for that submission.
cards.misconception: formAction adds a second Action to the form submission.

cards.statement: In React 19, a successful form Action automatically resets the form's uncontrolled fields.
cards.explanation: After a function form action succeeds, React resets uncontrolled field elements in that form.

cards.statement: In React 19, useFormStatus reports submission status for the form returned by its own component.
cards.explanation: useFormStatus from react-dom reads a parent form's status. Calling it in a component that renders the form does not track that form.
cards.misconception: useFormStatus tracks a form created in the same component.

cards.statement: In React 19, use(promise) shows a Suspense fallback while the Promise is pending.
cards.explanation: Reading a pending Promise with use suspends the component. A surrounding Suspense boundary shows its fallback until resolution.

cards.statement: In development, <StrictMode> runs a component's render code an extra time.
cards.explanation: <StrictMode> repeats render work in development to expose impure component logic.

cards.statement: In development, <StrictMode> runs an extra Effect setup and cleanup cycle.
cards.explanation: The extra setup and cleanup cycle helps reveal Effects whose cleanup fails to undo their setup.

cards.statement: In React 19, <StrictMode> invokes ref callbacks twice on initial mount during development.
cards.explanation: React 19 added this development-only check to simulate a mounted component being replaced by a Suspense fallback, so bugs surface before they ship.

cards.statement: In development, <StrictMode> wrapping only part of the app re-runs Effects on initial mount.
cards.explanation: If <StrictMode> is not at the app's root, React skips the extra Effect run on initial mount, since child Effects would double fire without their parents' Effects, which production never does.
cards.misconception: A partial-tree Strict Mode boundary repeats Effects on initial mount.

cards.statement: React identifies a component's Hook state by a stable call order across renders.
cards.explanation: Across renders of one component, React matches each Hook call to its state by call position. Stable ordering keeps those matches intact.

cards.statement: Calling useState inside an onClick handler follows the Rules of Hooks.
cards.explanation: Event handlers run in response to interactions, outside the component's rendering call where Hooks belong.
cards.misconception: An event handler is a valid place to call a Hook.

cards.statement: Under the Rules of Hooks, a fixed-count loop is an allowed place to call useState.
cards.explanation: Hooks are disallowed inside loops even when the iteration count appears fixed. Move the Hook call to a component or custom Hook's top level.
cards.misconception: A predictable loop length makes Hook calls inside the loop valid.

cards.statement: React's rules permit passing a custom Hook as a prop for the child to invoke.
cards.explanation: React's rules say to call a Hook directly inside a component or Hook. Passing a Hook as a prop for dynamic invocation is unsupported.
cards.misconception: A custom Hook can be passed as a prop for dynamic invocation.

cards.statement: eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags a useState call placed after a component's conditional early return.
cards.explanation: Hooks belong at the top level before any early return, so the rules-of-hooks lint reports a Hook after a conditional return as a violation.

cards.statement: Server Components run either once at build time or on a web server for each request.
cards.explanation: React's Server Component environment may be a build machine for static output or a web server handling requests.

cards.statement: Server Component rendering is the same step as server-side rendering to HTML.
cards.explanation: Server Components render before bundling. Their output can optionally undergo server-side rendering to produce HTML.
cards.misconception: Rendering Server Components and producing HTML through SSR are the same step.

cards.statement: The 'use client' directive marks a subtree of the render tree as client code.
cards.explanation: 'use client' creates a boundary in the module dependency tree; placement in the rendered component tree does not define that boundary.
cards.misconception: The client boundary follows the rendered parent-child tree.

cards.statement: A module that a 'use client' file imports is also treated as client code.
cards.explanation: Imports beneath a client-marked module run as client code even if those imported files have no directive.

cards.statement: A Server Component can pass a plain local callback as an onClick prop to a Client Component.
cards.explanation: Props crossing from a Server Component to a Client Component must be serializable; a plain local callback cannot cross that boundary.
cards.misconception: An ordinary locally defined callback can cross the server-client prop boundary.

cards.statement: A Client Component can receive a Server Component's rendered JSX through a prop.
cards.explanation: A Server Component can render JSX and pass the result as children or another prop for a Client Component to display.

cards.statement: Since React 19.3, a Server Component can render a Context imported from a 'use client' module.
cards.explanation: React 19.3 lets a Server Component import a Context from a 'use client' module and render it as a provider directly.

cards.statement: The 'use server' directive marks a module's components for server rendering.
cards.explanation: 'use server' marks Server Functions callable from client code. Server Components have no marking directive.
cards.misconception: The 'use server' directive identifies Server Components.

cards.statement: A Server Function becomes a Server Action when it is exported from a 'use server' module.
cards.explanation: A Server Function is called a Server Action when passed to an action prop or called from inside an action, regardless of its export location.
cards.misconception: Exporting from a 'use server' module determines the Server Action name.
